Newly emerged Common galaxias prolarvae are remarkably diminutive, measuring just 0.7 centimeters [Lb = 0.7 centimeters] in total length at birth immediately following eclosion. Hatching occurs after a developmental period heavily influenced by ambient thermal conditions, and the lecithotrophic alevin stage is brief, with the yolk sac being resorbed relatively quickly. The wet weight at birth is correspondingly minute, with each yolk-sac larva having a body mass of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture. This extremely low neonatal mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 1.0 millimeter (0.00052 grams) [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], places the newly hatched individual among the smallest of galaxiid larvae. These prolarvae remain largely passive, drifting in the water column as they rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The timing of this yolk-sac resorption and subsequent first feeding is critical, as a failure to transition to active prey capture within a suitable window can lead to high mortality during this vulnerable early life stage. Field observations confirm these diminutive dimensions are typical for the species across its broad geographic range.

As female Common galaxias undergo gonadal development, they must attain a threshold somatic size before reproductive maturation is possible. Detailed field surveys and laboratory growth studies indicate that the total length at puberty for females is 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to an age of several months post-hatching depending on local productivity and temperature regimes. Reaching this length marks the onset of vitellogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, enabling the first spawning event. Interestingly, this pubertal size is considerably smaller than the ultimate body dimensions the fish will eventually achieve, suggesting that energy allocation shifts only partially toward reproduction while somatic growth continues. In many populations, individuals at this size are still relatively slender and have not yet accumulated the lipid reserves seen in older, fully grown adults. The consistency of this 6.5 centimeter threshold across disparate habitats, from coastal streams to inland lakes, points to a genetically canalized maturation schedule, although the exact timing to reach this length can vary significantly with food availability and water temperature.

The maximum recorded body size for adult females of this species has been documented through extensive mark-recapture programs and museum specimen analyses. Under favourable conditions, female Common galaxias can attain a total length of 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters], representing the ultimate total length for females in most studied populations. This asymptotic dimension is typically reached after several years of sustained growth, with the most significant annual increases occurring during the first two growing seasons before the growth rate plateaus. Achieving this maximal length confers considerable fecundity advantages, as larger females can produce more numerous and larger oocytes per spawning event. Interestingly, males generally do not reach this same upper size limit, exhibiting somewhat smaller maximum dimensions. The 19 centimeter figure stands as a benchmark for assessing population health and habitat quality, as stunted growth or truncated size distributions often indicate resource limitation or high fishing pressure. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that this ultimate length is moderate for the genus, reflecting an intermediate life-history strategy.

Reproductive output in Common galaxias is strongly influenced by water temperature, and controlled laboratory experiments have quantified the species' maximum reproductive rate at a stable thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Under these conditions, individual females are capable of releasing approximately 37 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 37 oocytes per spawning event] during peak spawning periods, with spawning events occurring frequently throughout the extended breeding season. This remarkably high per-event fecundity is sustained by the species' iteroparous spawning strategy, where females release multiple small clutches over an extended reproductive window. The same 13 °C [T = 13 °C] thermal environment also appears to be near-optimal for other key physiological processes, including embryonic development and larval growth rates. Field collections of gravid females during the austral spring and summer months corroborate this laboratory-derived estimate, with individual ovarian masses indicating comparable oocyte production. This high fecundity is a classic characteristic of a small-bodied, short-lived, and highly fecund fish species that relies on numerical reproductive output to offset high early-life mortality in variable freshwater and estuarine environments.

Longevity data for Common galaxias, derived primarily from studies of the closely related Galaxias prognathus maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], indicate that the maximum documented lifespan is approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years], which classifies the species as a typical annual or short-lived perennial fish. Under natural conditions, very few individuals survive beyond their third or fourth year due to predation pressure, seasonal environmental extremes, and the energetic demands of repeated spawning events. The senescence process in older fish is marked by a gradual decline in condition factor, increased incidence of fin erosion, and reduced swimming performance. This maximum longevity is consistent with the species' overall life-history strategy of early maturation, high fecundity, and rapid generation turnover, which is well-suited to unpredictable freshwater habitats. Populations in cooler, more stable headwater streams may exhibit slightly longer average lifespans than those in warmer lower reaches, but the upper boundary appears to be fundamentally constrained by the species' physiology and reproductive schedule.
